title: Non-Slip Bath and Shower Mats: How to Pick One That Actually Grips
subtitle: A simple rubber mat is a low-cost bathroom safety fix, as long as it fits your tub, stays flat and is kept clean.
excerpt: Not every non-slip tub mat grips equally well. Here is how suction mats work, where they fall short, and what to check before you buy, with two examples listed at $15.29 and $18.99 (November 2026).
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: A wet tub or shower floor can be slippery. Add a little soap, a step over the tub edge, and legs that are not as steady as they used to be, and it is easy to see why many people think about bathroom safety.

One of the most basic fixes is also one of the simplest. The CDC STEADI "Check for Safety" checklist suggests a non-slip rubber mat or self-stick strips on the floor of the tub or shower. A mat is not a gadget in the high-tech sense. It is a practical household item that is worth choosing with a little care.
How non-slip mats work, and the two main kinds

Inside-the-tub mats usually grip in two ways. The underside is covered with small suction cups that press onto the tub floor and hold the mat in place. Many also have a textured top, such as a pebble pattern, so bare feet have something to hold on to.

Suction cups need a smooth surface to work. Both of the mats below are meant for smooth, non-textured tub and shower floors. Textured tile or a freshly refinished surface can defeat the suction. For a floor like that, the CDC checklist also mentions self-stick strips as an option.
Outside-the-tub mats are for the spot where you step out, dripping wet. Look for one with a flat rubber back. A fabric bath rug can slide, and it is not the same product.

Price is not a reliable guide to grip. In 2015, Hong Kong's Consumer Council tested 34 bath and shower mats that claimed to be slip resistant, and 9 of the 34 fell below the minimum requirement of the British standard it used. Passing and failing mats turned up across a wide price range. The Council put it this way:
"The slip resistance of 9 models fall below the minimum requirements set in the testing standard." — Consumer Council (Hong Kong), 2015

That test is older, so treat it as independent evidence rather than the last word. Still, the lesson holds: check how a mat is built rather than assuming a higher price means better grip. In that same 2015 Hong Kong test, rubber-backed mats generally met the slip-resistance requirement.

items: Size that matches the tub. The Consumer Council advises matching the mat's size to the tub so the edges do not roll up and trip you. Measure the flat floor of your tub before ordering.
Evenly spaced suction cups. The Council says uneven or sparse cups are a warning sign.
A smooth tub floor. Suction mats are made for smooth, non-textured surfaces.
A rubber back on any mat used outside the tub.
Cleaning instructions. Soap film, mildew and curled edges can weaken suction, so see whether the seller says the mat can be washed. The Lux page lists it as machine washable.
Returns and the seller. Check the return policy and who is selling the item, especially on store websites that also list outside sellers.

sections.content: Setting it up and keeping it safe
Clean the tub floor first, then lay the mat on a level surface and press so the suction cups hold. The Consumer Council suggests testing the suction on a level surface before relying on the mat.
After bathing, rinse the mat and let it dry. When you clean it, press the cups back down firmly when it goes back in. Bath oil reduces grip, so keep that in mind when you bathe.
Replace the mat if it is curled, torn or has lost cups. The Consumer Council advises replacing damaged or rolled-up mats.

A mat is a bathroom accessory, not a medical device, and it is not enough on its own for someone who needs a seat or stands unsteadily. It does nothing to help you stand up, sit down or step over the tub edge. For those moments, grab bars next to and inside the tub, and a bath seat if needed, are separate fixes. If you or a parent feel unsteady in the shower, talk with a doctor or physical therapist about what would help most.

sections.content: A well-fitted rubber mat is a modest step, and the two examples here are listed at $15.29 and $18.99 as of November 2026. Measure the tub, check that the floor is smooth, keep the mat clean and flat, and pair it with grab bars where they are needed.
